questions.q: A 35-year-old woman presents with a butterfly-shaped erythematous rash over the cheeks and nose sparing the nasolabial folds, joint pain, and photosensitivity. Which antibody is most specific for this diagnosis?
questions.exp: Anti-Sm (anti-Smith) antibody is the most specific antibody for SLE, though anti-dsDNA is more sensitive and correlates with disease activity. The malar rash sparing nasolabial folds is classic for SLE. Anti-histone is the hallmark of drug-induced lupus.

questions.q: A 28-year-old patient presents with grouped vesicles on an erythematous base over the right T5 dermatome preceded by 3 days of burning pain. The most appropriate first-line oral treatment is:
opts: Acyclovir 200 mg five times daily for 5 days
Valacyclovir 1000 mg three times daily for 7 days
Famciclovir 250 mg twice daily for 5 days
Acyclovir 400 mg three times daily for 5 days
questions.exp: Valacyclovir 1000 mg TDS for 7 days is the preferred oral agent for herpes zoster. It achieves 3-5x higher bioavailability than acyclovir and has been shown to reduce post-herpetic neuralgia. Treatment should begin within 72 hours of rash onset.

questions.q: A 6-year-old child presents with honey-coloured crusted lesions around the nose and mouth. Gram stain of the crust shows Gram-positive cocci in clusters. The most likely causative organism for the bullous variant is:
questions.exp: Bullous impetigo is caused almost exclusively by Staphylococcus aureus phage group II (especially phage type 71), which produces exfoliative toxin A. Non-bullous impetigo can be caused by either S. aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes. Honey-coloured crusting in the non-bullous form is more associated with S. pyogenes.

questions.q: A 50-year-old diabetic presents with tender, erythematous skin infection with crepitus on the foot. The most common type of necrotising fasciitis in this clinical context is:
opts: Type I — Group A Streptococcus alone
questions.exp: Necrotising fasciitis Type I (polymicrobial) is the most common form and typically occurs in diabetics, immunocompromised patients, and the elderly. It involves a synergistic combination of aerobic and anaerobic organisms. Type II is monomicrobial Group A Streptococcus and tends to affect healthy adults.

questions.q: A 22-year-old sexually active man presents with a painless, indurated, single ulcer on the glans penis. Darkfield microscopy of the serous exudate reveals corkscrew-motile spirochetes. The recommended treatment for this stage is:
opts: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM single dose
questions.exp: Primary syphilis (painless indurated chancre caused by Treponema pallidum) is treated with benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM as a single dose. This is the WHO and CDC standard of care. Doxycycline 100 mg BD for 14 days is the alternative for penicillin-allergic patients.

questions.q: A leprosy patient (borderline lepromatous) develops sudden onset painful nodular skin lesions, high fever, arthralgia, and orchitis. Nerve function remains intact. The pathophysiology of this reaction involves:
opts: Type III (immune complex) hypersensitivity — deposition in skin and vessels
Direct bacterial invasion causing tissue necrosis
questions.exp: Erythema Nodosum Leprosum (ENL/Type 2 reaction) is a Type III (immune complex-mediated) hypersensitivity reaction. Complement-fixing immune complexes of IgM/IgG with M. leprae antigens are deposited in tissues. It occurs in MB leprosy (BL/LL). Thalidomide is the drug of choice; prednisolone is used when thalidomide is contraindicated.

questions.q: A 30-year-old farmer presents with painless, progressive swelling of the foot with multiple discharging sinuses producing black granules. KOH mount shows large, dark, pigmented hyphae. The most common causative organism in India is:
questions.exp: Black-grain eumycetoma (fungal mycetoma) is most commonly caused by Madurella mycetomatis worldwide and in India. White-grain eumycetoma is caused by Scedosporium apiospermum or Acremonium species. Actinomadura madurae (white grains) and Nocardia brasiliensis (white/yellow grains) cause actinomycetoma (bacterial).

questions.q: A 55-year-old man presents with tense bullae on normal and erythematous skin predominantly affecting the trunk and flexures. Nikolsky sign is negative. Direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 at the dermoepidermal junction. The target antigen in this condition is:
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid (BP) targets BP180 (type XVII collagen, especially the NC16A domain) and BP230 at the hemidesmosome. Linear IgG/C3 at the BMZ on DIF and negative Nikolsky sign (subepidermal blister) are characteristic. ELISA for anti-BP180 NC16A is the most sensitive serological test.

questions.q: A 40-year-old woman presents with flaccid bullae rupturing to form painful oral and skin erosions. Nikolsky sign is positive. ELISA shows antibodies against desmoglein 3 (mucosa) and desmoglein 1 (skin). The most likely histological finding is:
opts: Suprabasal acantholysis with a 'row of tombstones' pattern
Neutrophilic microabscesses at dermal papillae tips
questions.exp: Pemphigus vulgaris shows suprabasal acantholysis — loss of adhesion between keratinocytes just above the basal layer, leaving the basal cells still attached to the BMZ like a 'row of tombstones'. The blister is intraepidermal. Direct IF shows intercellular IgG in a 'chicken-wire' pattern throughout the epidermis.

questions.q: A 7-year-old child has itchy, scaly patches on the scalp with hair loss and tender cervical lymphadenopathy. Wood's lamp examination shows bright green fluorescence. The systemic drug of choice and its duration is:
questions.exp: Tinea capitis requires systemic antifungals because topical agents cannot penetrate the hair shaft. Griseofulvin (10-15 mg/kg/day) for 6-8 weeks remains the drug of choice in children, particularly for Microsporum species. Green Wood's lamp fluorescence indicates Microsporum canis or M. audouinii (pteridine metabolites). Terbinafine is preferred for Trichophyton species.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman presents with well-demarcated, silvery-white plaques on the extensor elbows and scalp. Auspitz sign is positive. Which cytokine pathway is primarily responsible for the pathogenesis of psoriasis?
questions.exp: Psoriasis pathogenesis is driven primarily by the IL-23/Th17 axis. Dendritic cells produce IL-23, which drives naïve T cells to Th17 differentiation, producing IL-17A, IL-17F, and IL-22. These cytokines cause keratinocyte hyperproliferation. This explains why anti-IL-23 (risankizumab, guselkumab) and anti-IL-17 (secukinumab, ixekizumab) biologics are highly effective.

questions.q: A patient on long-term methotrexate for psoriasis has received a cumulative dose of 1.5 g. The most sensitive non-invasive marker for early hepatic fibrosis monitoring is:
opts: Serum ALT and AST levels every 3 months
Liver ultrasound with elastography every 6 months
questions.exp: Procollagen III peptide (PIIINP) is the most sensitive non-invasive serum marker of hepatic fibrosis for methotrexate monitoring. It correlates well with liver biopsy findings. Liver biopsy is recommended after a cumulative dose of 1.5-2 g or when PIIINP is persistently elevated. Routine LFTs are insensitive for early fibrosis.

questions.q: A 32-year-old woman with systemic sclerosis presents with progressive dyspnoea and diffuse skin thickening extending proximal to the elbows. The antibody most specific for diffuse cutaneous SSc with renal crisis is:
questions.exp: Anti-RNA polymerase III (anti-RNAP III) antibodies are strongly associated with diffuse cutaneous SSc and scleroderma renal crisis (SRC). Anti-Scl-70 is associated with diffuse SSc and pulmonary fibrosis. Anti-centromere is the hallmark of limited cutaneous SSc/CREST and is protective against renal crisis.

questions.q: A 38-year-old HIV-positive patient (CD4 = 90 cells/μL) presents with multiple pearly papules with central umbilication on the face and neck. The causative agent belongs to which virus family?
questions.exp: Molluscum contagiosum virus (MCV) belongs to the Poxviridae family, genus Molluscipoxvirus. It is the only member of its genus. In immunocompromised patients (HIV, CD4 <200), lesions are atypically large (>1 cm, 'giant molluscum'), numerous, and occur on atypical sites including the face. Treatment of underlying immunodeficiency is key.

questions.q: A leprosy patient on multidrug therapy develops sudden severe right-sided facial weakness, lagophthalmos, and loss of brow wrinkling. The nerve most commonly involved in leprosy causing this presentation is:
opts: Facial nerve (VII) at the zygomatic branch
Facial nerve (VII) at the main trunk
questions.exp: The facial (VII) nerve is the most commonly affected cranial nerve in leprosy. Involvement of the main trunk at the stylomastoid foramen or post-auricular branch causes lagophthalmos (failure to close eye), loss of brow wrinkling (frontalis), and corneal exposure risk. The greater auricular nerve is the most commonly thickened peripheral nerve in leprosy.

questions.q: A 52-year-old man presents with a pearly, translucent nodule with overlying telangiectasia on the inner canthus of the left eye that has slowly grown over 3 years. Dermoscopy shows arborising vessels. The MOST appropriate surgical management is:
opts: Wide local excision with 4 mm clinical margins
questions.exp: Basal cell carcinoma on the inner canthus (H-zone, high-risk area) requires Mohs micrographic surgery. The H-zone (central face, nasal ala, inner canthus, ear) demands tissue-sparing maximum margin control. Mohs offers >99% cure rate for primary facial BCC vs ~90% for standard excision. Arborising vessels on dermoscopy are pathognomonic for BCC.

questions.q: A 60-year-old woman with a 20-year history of venous ulcer develops a rapidly growing, fungating ulcer with raised everted edges that bleeds on contact. Biopsy shows well-differentiated SCC. This transformation is called:
questions.exp: Marjolin's ulcer is malignant transformation (most commonly SCC) arising in chronic wounds, scars, or inflammatory conditions: burn scars (latency 20-30 years), chronic venous ulcers, osteomyelitis sinuses, vaccination scars. It carries a worse prognosis than de novo SCC due to higher metastatic rate (~30%) because it lacks lymphatics in scar tissue.

questions.q: A 26-year-old man develops classic target lesions on the palms and soles 10 days after a cold sore. Individual lesions show three concentric zones: central dusky area, pale oedematous ring, and peripheral erythema. No mucosal involvement. This best represents:
questions.exp: Erythema multiforme (EM) minor is characterised by classic 'target' or 'iris' lesions on acral sites with no or minimal mucosal involvement (<1 mucosal site). HSV-1 and HSV-2 are the most common triggers (>80%). EM major involves ≥2 mucosal sites. EM is now separated from SJS/TEN — SJS has >10% BSA detachment and is usually drug-induced.

questions.q: During patch testing, a positive reaction at 48h that further intensifies at 96h (crescendo pattern) indicates allergic contact dermatitis. A reaction that is positive at 48h but fades by 96h (decrescendo pattern) indicates:
questions.exp: Irritant contact dermatitis (ICD) patch test reactions typically peak at 48h and decrease by 96h (decrescendo/fading pattern) because they are non-immunological, concentration-dependent reactions. In contrast, allergic contact dermatitis (ACD) reactions increase from 48h to 96-120h (crescendo pattern) due to the immunological amplification phase. This distinction is critical in interpreting patch tests.

questions.q: A 38-year-old woman presents with bilateral hyperpigmented patches on the cheeks, upper lip, and forehead worsening in summer. She is on oral contraceptive pills. Wood's lamp examination enhances the pigmentation. This indicates pigment is predominantly in the:
questions.exp: Wood's lamp (365 nm UVA) enhances epidermal pigmentation (appears darker) but does not enhance dermal pigmentation. In melasma, the epidermal type (Wood's lamp positive) has the best response to treatment. Mixed type (epidermal + dermal) has intermediate response. Dermal type responds poorly. OCPs and UV light are the main triggers.

questions.q: A 45-year-old HIV-positive man (CD4 = 80 cells/μL) presents with purplish violaceous plaques on the lower legs, oral palate, and gastrointestinal tract. Biopsy shows spindle cell proliferation with slit-like vascular channels and extravasated erythrocytes. The causative virus and its primary route of transmission is:
questions.exp: Kaposi's sarcoma is caused by HHV-8 (KSHV — Kaposi's Sarcoma-associated Herpesvirus). In HIV-positive men who have sex with men, sexual transmission (primarily via saliva) is the main route. HAART is the cornerstone of AIDS-KS management; it reduces KS incidence by 80%. Chemotherapy (liposomal doxorubicin) is used for advanced disease.

questions.q: A patient with tinea cruris fails 4 weeks of topical clotrimazole. The active lesion extends beyond the natal cleft. The most effective topical antifungal for dermatophytes that is fungicidal (not fungistatic) is:
questions.exp: Terbinafine (allylamine class) is fungicidal against dermatophytes by inhibiting squalene epoxidase, causing lethal accumulation of squalene. Azoles (clotrimazole, econazole, miconazole) are fungistatic, inhibiting ergosterol synthesis via CYP51. Terbinafine 1% cream applied twice daily for 1-2 weeks achieves higher cure rates than azoles for tinea corporis/cruris/pedis.

questions.q: A 65-year-old farmer presents with slow-growing, verrucous plaque on the foot with nodular satellites and discharging sinuses over 10 years. Biopsy shows pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia with brown pigmented round cells dividing by binary fission. These cells are called:
questions.exp: Chromoblastomycosis (chromomycosis) is characterised by sclerotic bodies (Medlar bodies/copper penny bodies) — brown, thick-walled, septate cells that reproduce by planate division (binary fission in a single plane). These are pathognomonic. Causative agents: Fonsecaea pedrosoi (most common), Cladophialophora carrionii. Treatment: itraconazole ± terbinafine for 6-12 months.

questions.q: A dermatology resident performs a Tzanck smear from the floor of a fresh blister in a patient with pemphigus vulgaris. The finding on Tzanck smear in pemphigus vulgaris is:
opts: Multinucleated giant cells with nuclear molding
Acantholytic cells (rounded, large, with prominent nuclei) — Tzanck cells
No diagnostic finding — Tzanck is not useful in PV
questions.exp: In pemphigus vulgaris, Tzanck smear shows acantholytic keratinocytes (Tzanck cells) — rounded cells that have lost their adhesion, with enlarged nuclei and prominent nucleoli, and abundant basophilic cytoplasm. Unlike herpes, there are NO multinucleated giant cells. Tzanck smear is a quick bedside test to confirm acantholysis.

questions.q: A 20-year-old woman presents with diffuse hair shedding of 200+ hairs/day beginning 3 months after delivery of a healthy baby. Pull test is strongly positive. Trichoscopy shows no miniaturisation. The expected natural course is:
opts: Evolution into female pattern hair loss
questions.exp: Postpartum telogen effluvium (TE) is a self-limiting condition. During pregnancy, high oestrogen prolongs the anagen (growth) phase. After delivery, oestrogen drops precipitously, triggering synchronous telogen entry of retained hairs, leading to shedding 2-4 months later. It resolves spontaneously within 6-12 months. Reassurance is the main treatment. No miniaturisation distinguishes it from FPHL.

questions.q: A patient with dermatophyte toenail onychomycosis (distal subungual type, 3 nails, no matrix involvement) fails topical therapy. The drug of choice and regimen is:
opts: Fluconazole 150 mg once weekly for 6 months
questions.exp: Terbinafine 250 mg daily is the first-line systemic treatment for dermatophyte onychomycosis with the highest mycological cure rates. Duration: 6 weeks for fingernails, 12 weeks for toenails. It is fungicidal (vs fungistatic azoles). Itraconazole pulse (400 mg/day for 1 week/month) is preferred for Candida onychomycosis. Griseofulvin has poor nail penetration.

questions.q: A 40-year-old woman on long-term hydroxychloroquine for cutaneous lupus has developed progressive visual field defects. Ophthalmology reports 'bull's eye maculopathy'. The safe maximum daily dose to minimise retinal toxicity is:
questions.exp: Per AAO 2016 guidelines, the safe daily dose of hydroxychloroquine to minimise retinal toxicity is ≤5 mg/kg/day of actual body weight (not ideal body weight). Above this threshold, cumulative toxicity risk increases significantly. Annual ophthalmological screening (visual field + SD-OCT) is mandatory from baseline or after 5 years. Bull's eye maculopathy is an irreversible, late finding.

questions.q: A patient with lepromatous leprosy presents with collapse of the nasal bridge (saddle-nose deformity). The pathological basis of this nasal involvement is:
opts: Peripheral nerve invasion causing sensory loss and trauma
Direct bacillary infiltration and destruction of the anterior nasal cartilage and bones
Type 1 reversal reaction targeting nasal mucosa
questions.exp: In lepromatous leprosy (LL), the nasal mucosa is heavily infiltrated with bacilli (rich in M. leprae as it is a cooler site). Progressive destruction of the anterior nasal spine, septal cartilage, and inferior turbinates leads to saddle-nose deformity. The nasal smear in LL patients shows high BI. This is a feature of longstanding, untreated LL.

questions.q: A 33-year-old man with severe atopic dermatitis unresponsive to moderate-potency topical corticosteroids is started on dupilumab. The primary molecular target of dupilumab is:
opts: IL-4 receptor alpha subunit (IL-4Rα), blocking IL-4 and IL-13 signalling
questions.exp: Dupilumab is a fully human monoclonal antibody targeting the IL-4 receptor alpha (IL-4Rα) subunit, which is shared by the IL-4 and IL-13 receptor complexes. By blocking IL-4Rα, it simultaneously inhibits both IL-4 and IL-13 signalling — the core Th2 cytokines driving atopic dermatitis inflammation. It is approved for moderate-to-severe AD, eosinophilic oesophagitis, and prurigo nodularis.

questions.q: A 48-year-old woman presents with intensely pruritic grouped papulovesicles on the extensor elbows, knees, and buttocks. Biopsy shows neutrophilic microabscesses at dermal papillae tips. DIF shows granular IgA deposits at dermal papillae. The most appropriate confirmatory investigation for the underlying enteropathy is:
opts: Anti-tissue transglutaminase IgA (anti-tTG IgA) + duodenal biopsy
questions.exp: Dermatitis herpetiformis (DH) is the cutaneous manifestation of coeliac disease (gluten-sensitive enteropathy). Granular IgA at dermal papillae on DIF is pathognomonic. Anti-tissue transglutaminase (tTG) IgA is the most sensitive serological marker for coeliac disease (sensitivity >95%), and duodenal biopsy confirms villous atrophy. Dapsone controls skin symptoms; strict gluten-free diet treats the underlying enteropathy.

questions.q: A 28-year-old man from Rajasthan presents with a slow-growing cutaneous nodule on the forearm that has developed into a painless ulcer with raised, undermined edges and a 'volcano crater' appearance. He has a history of travel to the Thar desert region. The causative organism and its vector is:
opts: Leishmania tropica or L. major — Phlebotomus sandfly
questions.exp: Cutaneous leishmaniasis in India (Oriental sore) is caused by Leishmania tropica (urban, dry type) or L. major (rural, moist type), transmitted by Phlebotomus sandflies. L. donovani causes visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar). L. braziliensis causes mucocutaneous leishmaniasis in South America (Lutzomyia vector). Treatment: intralesional sodium stibogluconate or miltefosine.
